questions.explanation: Gk. 'akron' = peak/top (as in 'Acropolis' = high city). Phobia-cluster: acrophobia = heights. Distractors deliberately chosen from the same cluster so a student who has only skimmed gets tripped.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: L. 'claustrum' = enclosed place; hence fear of confinement. Pair it mentally with agoraphobia (fear of OPEN spaces) — these are opposites and are often tested together as a trap pair.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: XENOPHOBIA is the fear or hatred of:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'xenos' = stranger. Antonym: xenophile (lover of foreigners). Extremely high-hit in editorials, SSC reading comprehension, and banking synonym questions.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: Gk. 'hydor' = water. Note double meaning: (i) psychological fear of water, (ii) a clinical symptom of rabies. Both senses appear in PYQs.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: Gk. 'nyx / nyctos' = night. Its opposite, photophobia, is fear of LIGHT — another paper-setter pair. Distractor 'sleep' is hypnophobia; 'death' is thanatophobia.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The fear of public speaking is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'glossa' = tongue (also root of 'glossary'). Glossophobia is tested repeatedly in soft-skills vocabulary. Graphophobia is fear of writing; ochlophobia is fear of crowds.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: Gk. 'ophis' = snake. Often confused with arachnophobia (spiders) and entomophobia (insects). All three are separate; the paper-setter's favourite trap is testing them side-by-side.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.explanation: Gk. 'thanatos' = death; also the root of 'euthanasia' (literally 'good death'). A high-hit word in editorial vocab.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A person who hates foreigners is a:
questions.explanation: The -phobe suffix marks the hater (as -phile marks the lover). Xenophile loves foreigners; misanthrope hates all mankind; philanthrope (philanthropist) loves mankind. Paper-setter's delight — the antonym cluster.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Fear of the number 13 is called:
questions.explanation: Gk. 'treis-kai-deka' = three and ten = 13. Appears in SSC CGL and banking vocab lists as a 'memorable' trap word. Tetraphobia is fear of 4 (common in East Asia); arithmophobia is fear of numbers generally.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: ARACHNOPHOBIA is the intense and irrational fear of which group of creatures?

options.option_text: insects including flies, ants, and beetles
reptiles such as lizards and crocodiles
birds of prey such as eagles and falcons

questions.explanation: Arachnophobia derives from the Greek 'arachne' meaning spider. Option A is the most common trap: spiders are arachnids, not insects — both are arthropods, but insects have six legs while arachnids have eight, making the distinction exam-critical.

questions.stem: AGORAPHOBIA is best described as the persistent fear of:

options.option_text: confined, enclosed, and narrow indoor spaces
open spaces, crowds, and public environments
social interactions and formal gathering events
travelling alone in unfamiliar distant territories

questions.explanation: Agoraphobia comes from Greek 'agora' (marketplace or open assembly place), denoting fear of open or crowded public spaces. Option A describes Claustrophobia (fear of enclosed spaces) — the single most common distractor examiners plant for this term.

questions.stem: A passenger who refuses to board an aircraft due to an intense dread of flying is most likely suffering from:

options.option_text: Acrophobia — an irrational terror of high altitudes
Aerophobia — a specific and persistent dread of flying
Agoraphobia — anxiety caused by crowded open spaces
Claustrophobia — panic triggered by confined cabin spaces

questions.explanation: Aerophobia (Greek 'aero' = air) is fear specifically of flying or air travel. Option A (Acrophobia) is the classic trap: many assume flight fear equals height fear, but Acrophobia is triggered by standing at heights on the ground, not by the act of flying.

questions.stem: MYSOPHOBIA, sometimes popularly called 'germophobia', is an extreme and debilitating fear of:

options.option_text: contamination by germs and infectious microorganisms
decaying food items and organic decomposition odours
polluted water bodies and toxic chemical spillages
touching dirty soil, mud, and garden compost heaps

questions.explanation: Mysophobia derives from Greek 'mysos' meaning uncleanness or contamination, and refers specifically to fear of germs or microbial infection. Options B–D describe disgust-adjacent reactions but are not the precise referent; Mysophobia is generalised germ-contamination dread, not dirt or smell aversion.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly defines CYNOPHOBIA?

options.option_text: intense and irrational fear of dogs specifically
extreme aversion to wild wolves and predatory foxes
persistent dread of domestic cats and all household pets
general anxiety and panic around large wild mammals

questions.explanation: Cynophobia comes from Greek 'kyon' (dog) and refers exclusively to fear of dogs. Option B is the most plausible trap: wolves are canids and share the root, but cynophobia is dog-specific. Option C (cats) belongs to Ailurophobia, another PYQ-frequent term.

questions.stem: The morbid fear of needles and hypodermic syringes — which often prevents patients from seeking medical care — is called:

options.option_text: Haemophobia — irrational terror of blood and open wounds
Iatrophobia — persistent and generalised fear of doctors
Trypanophobia — intense dread of needles and injections
Algophobia — extreme and disabling sensitivity to physical pain

questions.explanation: Trypanophobia derives from Greek 'trypanon' (borer or piercing instrument), specifically denoting needle/injection fear. Option A (Haemophobia = blood fear) is the primary distractor because the two co-occur in clinical settings, but they are categorically distinct phobias — a distinction frequently tested in higher-difficulty papers.

questions.stem: ERGOPHOBIA, derived from the Greek root 'ergon' meaning 'work', denotes the persistent fear of:

options.option_text: monotonous and physically exhausting industrial labour
workplaces, work itself, or performing occupational tasks
competitive professional environments and career rivalries
technological machinery and automated industrial equipment

questions.explanation: Ergophobia (from 'ergon' = work + 'phobos' = fear) covers the broad fear of work in any form — the workplace, the act of working, or performing tasks — not limited to physical or exhausting labour as Option A implies. Options C and D describe narrower workplace anxieties that have no corresponding classical phobia term, making B the only etymologically and clinically accurate choice.
